h1: The 6 Best Kindle Alternatives of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six e-readers that beat the Kindle on library borrowing, file formats, color screens or Android freedom, sorted by use.
summary: The Kobo Libra Colour is the best Kindle alternative, with a 7-inch Kaleido 3 color screen, physical page-turn buttons and built-in OverDrive and Libby borrowing. The PocketBook Verse Pro is the pick for big file libraries, and the InkPad Color 3 has the largest color page. The Verse Pro Color and Verse cover compact and budget needs, and the OBOOK6 runs Android apps for the least money.
intro: People leaving the Kindle usually shop for a better screen and forget that the real lock-in is the library. Before buying anything, work out where your books live: Amazon purchases, a public library app, or a folder of files you bought elsewhere. The device that reads those books without friction is the right one, however good a rival's screen looks in a photo.

Our editors compared six e-readers from their listings, scored on the Primea framework, with library borrowing, file format support, color or black and white, page-turn controls and software design weighted most. Prices appear as buckets only. None of these opens an Amazon purchase natively except the Android-based OBOOK6, so check your library first, because the cheapest reader is the one that opens your books.

products.name: Kobo Libra Colour, 7" Glare-Free Colour E Ink Kaleido 3, Waterproof, Black
products.verdict: The closest thing to a better Kindle for people who borrow library books.
products.description:
The Libra Colour pairs a 7-inch Kaleido 3 color E Ink screen with physical page-turn buttons and built-in OverDrive and Libby support. It is waterproof, and it costs $200 to $500. Built-in library support means you borrow a book from your public library on the device, with no sideloading or computer needed.

The top spot goes to it as the only pick here that combines buttons, color and native library borrowing. The InkPad Color 3 has a larger page, but no page-turn buttons, and the PocketBook models lack built-in library apps.

Buy it if you borrow from a library and want a Kindle-like experience with better openness. The caveats are the priciest bracket and color text that is less crisp than black and white. Skip it if you buy mostly from Amazon.
cons: Color panel less crisp than black and white
products.idealFor: Library borrowers who want buttons and color.
products.skipIf: You buy mostly from Amazon and want its store.

products.name: PocketBook Verse Pro E-Reader Waterproof, 6" E-Ink Carta HD, Azure
products.verdict: Opens nearly any file you already own, with no conversion.
products.description:
The Verse Pro has a 6-inch E Ink Carta HD display, waterproofing, text-to-speech, and both Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. Its standout is broad format support, and it costs $100 to $200. Carta HD is a sharper black-and-white panel than the color Kaleido screens, which suits novels.

Second place fits because file freedom is what most people leaving Kindle actually want, and the Verse Pro opens nearly any file you own. It lacks the Libra's built-in library borrowing and buttons, but it undercuts it by a price bracket.

Buy it if you have a large folder of non-Kindle files. The caveats are the small 6-inch screen and no color option. Skip it if you want color or a larger page.
products.idealFor: Readers with a large folder of non-Kindle files.
products.skipIf: You want color or a larger page.

products.name: PocketBook InkPad Color 3, 7.8" Color E-Paper Display, Waterproof
products.verdict: The roomiest color page among the closed-system readers.
products.description:
The InkPad Color 3 has a 7.8-inch color E-paper display, a built-in speaker, 32GB of storage, and a waterproof body, at $200 to $500. Color matters for comics, maps and textbooks, where a gray page loses information, and the speaker supports audio features.

Third place reflects that the larger page suits comics, textbooks and PDFs, yet it costs about as much as the Libra Colour while offering fewer reading conveniences. A bigger page helps technical documents but is awkward in one hand.

Buy it if comics and PDFs are your main reading. The caveats are the bulk for one-handed reading and the costly bracket. Skip it if you want a pocketable reader.

products.name: PocketBook Verse Pro Color, 6" E Ink Kaleido 3, IPX8 Waterproof
products.verdict: Color without the Android fiddling, at a mid price.
products.description:
This is a 6-inch Kaleido 3 color E Ink reader with an IPX8 waterproof rating and a closed, simple software system, for $100 to $200. IPX8 is a strong immersion rating, so a drop in the bath is survivable. A closed system means no Android tinkering: it opens and works.

It lands below the black-and-white Verse Pro since color panels trade sharpness for hue, but it undercuts the larger color readers on price. Against the OBOOK6, it is easier to live with.

Buy it for cheap color in a small body. The caveats are the smaller color page and no Android apps. Skip it if you need the crispest black text, where the Verse Pro is better.
products.idealFor: Readers who want cheap color in a small body.
products.skipIf: You need the crispest black text.

products.name: PocketBook Verse E-Reader, 6" E-Ink Carta HD, Bright Blue
products.verdict: File freedom and a memory card slot for the least money in the Pocketbook line.
products.description:
The standard Verse has a 6-inch Carta HD screen, broad format support, a memory card slot, and up to a month of battery per the listing, at $100 to $200. A memory card slot adds storage cheaply, which the Libra Colour does not allow.

Fifth place comes from how it gives up the waterproofing and extras of the Verse Pro, though it keeps the format freedom. For readers who never take a book near water, the loss is small.

Buy it if you want file freedom and expandable storage on a budget. The caveats are no listed waterproofing and no color. Skip it if you read near water, because the Verse Pro covers that.
products.idealFor: Budget readers with files to open.

products.name: OBOOK6 eReader (32GB), 6" 300ppi Glare-Free Display, Android
products.verdict: The cheapest way to put real Android apps on an E Ink screen.
products.description:
The OBOOK6 runs genuine Android on a 6-inch 300ppi glare-free display with 32GB of storage for $50 to $100, the lowest here. Genuine Android means you can install the Kindle app or any other reading app, which the closed systems cannot do.

Last place follows because open Android on a low-cost device is a project, not an appliance, and it comes from a lesser-known brand. Battery life suffers on Android compared with the closed readers.

Buy it for a budget reader that runs your own apps. The caveats are setup effort and a lesser-known brand. Skip it if you want a polished plug-and-play device.
products.idealFor: Budget readers who want their own apps.
products.skipIf: You want a polished plug-and-play device.

whatMatters.detail: OverDrive and Libby let you borrow ebooks free from a public library. Some readers include the apps and others need sideloading. Look for the named apps in the product bullets, as with the Kobo Libra Colour, and check that your library system supports the service. Most do, but wait lists apply to popular titles.

Kindle devices are fussy about formats other than Amazon's. Readers with broad support open EPUB and similar files directly. Check the format list on the listing, and remember that DRM-protected purchases from one store do not open on another store's device without a conversion step. Open formats such as EPUB avoid the problem entirely.

Color E Ink adds hue but slightly dulls the contrast and sharpness of text. It helps for comics and covers. Look for Kaleido in the title and expect softer text than a black-and-white Carta panel. If you mostly read novels, color is a cost with little benefit. Gray pages also refresh faster and read sharper.

Buttons let you flip pages without touching the screen, useful one-handed or with gloves. Touch-only readers can feel clumsy. The listing will mention physical buttons if present, and only the Libra Colour here has them, which is a real comfort advantage for long sessions, since touch-only screens smudge and tire your thumb.

Android lets you install any reading app but requires setup and drains battery faster. A closed system works at once. Check whether the listing says Android, and if you want the Kindle app on the device, the OBOOK6 is the only pick here that supports it. Everything else needs a different route, such as the Kindle app on a tablet.

howToChoose.intro: Your existing library is the strongest guide.

cards.label: Color
cards.text: Good for covers, comics and charts but softer for text. The Kobo Libra Colour, InkPad Color 3 and Verse Pro Color use it.

cards.label: Black and white
cards.text: Sharper and cheaper for novels. The PocketBook Verse Pro, Verse and OBOOK6 use it.

howToChoose.note: Most novel readers should default to black and white.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Named OverDrive or Libby support in the listing bullets.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: The Kobo Libra Colour lists built-in OverDrive and Libby, making it the straightforward choice.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You want library borrowing, buttons and color together; the Kobo Libra Colour delivers all three.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You read plain text novels; the PocketBook Verse or OBOOK6 is enough.

faq.a: Not natively on Kobo or PocketBook. The Android-based OBOOK6 can run the Kindle app, so it is the route if you have a large Amazon library. Expect more setup and shorter battery life than a closed reader.

faq.q: Which one works with my public library?
faq.a: The Kobo Libra Colour lists built-in OverDrive and Libby support, so you borrow library books directly from your account without a computer. The PocketBook readers rely on other methods, such as sideloading files.

faq.q: Is color E Ink worth it over black and white?
faq.a: Only for comics and illustrated books. Text looks softer, so novel readers should skip it and take the Verse Pro or Verse instead. Color is a bonus only for visual books.

faq.q: Do I need to convert my files?
faq.a: The PocketBook Verse line lists broad format support, so most files open directly. A Kindle would need conversion first, which is a chore the Verse avoids. That saves time if you own many EPUB files.

The Kobo Libra Colour, Verse Pro, Verse Pro Color and InkPad Color 3 are listed as waterproof. The standard Verse and the OBOOK6 do not list waterproofing, so keep them away from the bath and the pool. A splash is not the same as a dunk.

faq.q: Is the OBOOK6 a good idea?
faq.a: It is a budget Android device with a lesser-known brand. It suits people who like tinkering and want the Kindle app on an E Ink screen. Expect a quirkier experience than a Kobo.

finalTake: Buy the Kobo Libra Colour if you borrow from a public library and want buttons and color, and the PocketBook Verse Pro if you already own a folder of non-Kindle files. The InkPad Color 3 suits comics and textbooks, while the Verse Pro Color and Verse cover compact and budget needs. The OBOOK6 is for tinkerers who want Android apps, including the Kindle app.
